content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) convened a workshop in Atlanta from March 26 to 28, 1991, to address the prevention of chlamydial infections. Experts in the field participated in this workshop to provide technical and scientific insights. Chlamydia trachomatis infections are highly prevalent among sexually active adolescents and young adults in the United States, with over 4 million cases occurring annually. The infection is often insidious, as most infected women and many men exhibit no symptoms or only mild symptoms. This asymptomatic population contributes significantly to the ongoing transmission of the infection within communities. Furthermore, these individuals are at risk of developing acute illnesses and severe long-term complications. Historically, the prevention and management of chlamydial infections were hindered by the lack of effective laboratory tests for screening and diagnosis. However, advancements in diagnostic testing now enable better detection and management. Through education, screening, partner referral, and appropriate patient care, public health professionals and healthcare providers can work together to reduce the morbidity and economic burden associated with this infection. Prevalence of Chlamydial Infection Adolescents and young adults are at a particularly high risk of acquiring chlamydial infections. Studies indicate that age is the most significant sociodemographic factor associated with infection, with prevalence rates exceeding 10% among sexually active adolescent females. Higher prevalence rates are also observed among individuals living in inner cities, those with lower socioeconomic status, and Black populations. However, prevalence rates of at least 5% are consistent across all regions, regardless of urban or rural settings, race, or ethnicity. Fewer studies have focused on men, but prevalence rates exceeding 5% have been reported among young men seeking healthcare for non-genitourinary reasons. Research from North America and Europe has identified chlamydial infections in male high school students, military personnel, semen donors, adolescents in detention centers, and young men attending adolescent clinics or university health centers. Clinical Spectrum of Chlamydial Infection in Nonpregnant Women Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is the most serious acute complication of chlamydial infection, accounting for significant morbidity and economic costs. Treating women with acute, symptomatic PID is insufficient as a prevention strategy, as treatment does not always prevent complications, and many women with tubal infections have symptoms too mild or nonspecific to seek medical care. Chlamydial infection typically begins at the cervix, with the urethra and rectum also being potential sites of infection. Symptoms, when present, may include vaginal discharge and dysuria. If untreated, the infection can ascend to the endometrium and fallopian tubes, causing lower abdominal pain and menstrual irregularities. Untreated infections often persist for months, during which complications may develop, and transmission to others may occur. Approximately 8% of women with chlamydial infections develop overt salpingitis. In cases of dual gonococcal and chlamydial infections where only gonorrhea was treated, 30% of women developed salpingitis during follow-up. Chlamydia has been isolated in 5% to 50% of women presenting with PID symptoms. Annually, PID results in 5 million outpatient visits, over 275,000 hospitalizations, and more than 100,000 surgical procedures. The long-term consequences of PID include infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy. Approximately 17% of women treated for PID become infertile, and 10% of those who conceive experience ectopic pregnancies. Studies have shown that undetected and untreated tubal infections are a major cause of infertility and ectopic pregnancies. Clinical Spectrum of Chlamydial Infection in Infants Nearly two-thirds of infants born vaginally to mothers with chlamydial infections acquire the infection during delivery. Despite prophylaxis with silver nitrate or antibiotic ointments, 15% to 25% of exposed infants develop chlamydial conjunctivitis, and 3% to 16% develop chlamydial pneumonia. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis and a significant cause of pneumonia in the first few months of life. Infants with chlamydial pneumonia are at increased risk of abnormal pulmonary function later in childhood. Clinical Spectrum of Chlamydial Infection in Men In men, urethritis is the most common manifestation of chlamydial infection. However, complications are rare. Asymptomatic men may unknowingly transmit the infection to their sexual partners. Symptoms, when present, include urethral discharge and dysuria, but they are often mild or absent compared to gonorrheal urethritis. Chlamydial infections account for 30% to 40% of non-gonococcal urethritis cases and 50% of epididymitis cases among adolescent and young adult males. These infections respond well to antibiotic treatment. Prevention Strategies The primary goal of chlamydia prevention is to prevent both symptomatic and asymptomatic salpingitis and its complications. Secondary goals include preventing perinatal and postpartum infections and other adverse outcomes. Prevention programs should include both primary and secondary prevention strategies. Primary Prevention Primary prevention focuses on reducing the risk of acquiring chlamydial infections through behavioral changes, such as delaying sexual activity, reducing the number of sexual partners, and using barrier contraception. Identifying and treating infected individuals before they transmit the infection to others is critical. Active screening and partner referral are essential components of primary prevention. Secondary Prevention Secondary prevention aims to prevent complications among those already infected. This includes screening asymptomatic individuals, treating infected individuals and their partners, and recognizing clinical conditions associated with chlamydia, such as mucopurulent cervicitis and urethral syndrome. Target Populations Adolescents and young adults are at the highest risk for chlamydial infections. Prevention efforts should focus on sexually active adolescents and young adults, regardless of geographic or socioeconomic factors. Healthcare providers should be actively involved in these efforts. Laboratory Testing Advances in non-culture diagnostic tests, such as enzyme immunoassays and nucleic acid hybridization tests, have facilitated widespread screening. These tests are easier to perform and less expensive than culture tests, making them suitable for large-scale screening programs. However, non-culture tests may produce false-positive results, and all positive results should be confirmed with additional testing. Proper specimen collection and handling are critical for accurate diagnosis. Clinicians should be trained to collect specimens from the endocervix in women and the urethra in men.
